title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Wixom tightens rules on data centers despite lawsuit threat from developers.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. It's Sunday, August 30, and we're starting the day with a close look at one suburb's push to get ahead of these massive projects.
That's right, Emmy. Today the big story is out of Wixom, where city officials just advanced new restrictions on data centers even as a developer lawsuit hangs over them.
What exactly did they do this week?
On August 26 the council passed zoning changes that set a 1,500-foot setback from homes, parks, and schools, plus requirements for noise studies, water usage limits, and other standards.
They also ended their six-month moratorium early, right?
Yes, the new rules kick in no later than September 6, wrapping up the pause that started back in March.
Why move so fast on the rules while the moratorium was still in place?
Officials wanted to lock in protections before the pause expired and give themselves a stronger position.
This isn't happening in a vacuum. How long has Wixom been wrestling with this?
The planning commission started reviewing data center rules last November after the council directed them to look at the zoning ordinance.
And the moratorium came in March when they realized they needed more time.
Exactly. Wixom isn't alone — more than twenty Michigan communities have used similar pauses this year to study power, water, and noise impacts.
Who is the developer behind the lawsuit?
Wixom Industrial One, tied to Missouri-based Sansone Group. They want to build a roughly 519,000-square-foot facility on 54 acres along South Wixom Road.
What are they arguing in court?
The suit claims the moratorium is illegal and was designed to kill their project after the city had been working with them on plans.
How does this fit into the bigger picture across the state?
Data centers are drawing huge interest because of tax incentives passed in 2024, but they're also massive users of electricity and water for cooling.
What kind of numbers are we talking about?

A single large facility can pull hundreds of megawatts to over a gigawatt and millions of gallons of water a day, which is why utilities like DTE are planning new gas plants and seeing an 8-gigawatt pipeline.
That demand is already showing up in rate cases, isn't it?
Yes, and it ties directly into why residents in places like Wixom are pushing back on local taxes, traffic, and utility bills.
What happens next in Wixom with the lawsuit pending?
The city will defend the new ordinance in federal court, and the developer is asking a judge to let their site plan move forward anyway.
Could this chill other projects or encourage more towns to write their own rules?
That's the open question — whether the legal fight deters investment or simply forces clearer standards everywhere.
Residents seem pretty vocal from what I've seen.
They've been showing up at meetings thanking the council for holding the line and calling the lawsuit corporate pressure.
So the stakes are really about local control versus rapid development.
And about who pays the infrastructure costs if these facilities come online.
Any sense of how many other Oakland County towns are watching this?
At least a couple nearby suburbs have already tightened their own zoning this summer after similar resident concerns.
It feels like a pattern that's spreading fast.
And that's why today's Wixom vote matters beyond just one city.
We'll keep tracking the court case and how other communities respond.
Now let's run through the rest of the week's developments in quick hits.
Yesterday Ellington Township in Tuscola County approved a moratorium on new data centers to study power and water demands.
That gives residents time before any large projects move ahead.
Also yesterday a Genesee County committee delivered its impact study on data centers to local leaders.
Officials now have details on potential strain to power, water, and roads that could affect taxpayers.
On Friday Attorney General Dana Nessel told regulators she wants a 71 percent cut to DTE's requested $474 million rate hike.
Data center power demand is one reason DTE cited for the increase.
Lawmakers also introduced new state bills Friday aimed at regulating large data center builds.
The measures would add oversight on power use, noise, and local tax agreements.
A recall effort against officials who approved a big tech facility failed on Friday after the clerk rejected the petitions.
That keeps the 500-acre project on track in a divided community.
The Saline Township project is still advancing despite new local rules and pushback.
It could bring construction jobs but also heavy utility demands.
Thursday DTE said it will seek approval for two new natural gas plants to meet data center demand.
That comes as older coal units retire and could affect customer bills.
Two more Metro Detroit towns also updated zoning Thursday to curb data centers after resident concerns over noise and resources.
And earlier in the week a developer sued Wixom after the city blocked its project.
That case is now part of the ongoing legal back-and-forth we talked about in the main story.
For on deck, no public meetings are currently listed for the next couple of days on the tracker.
Listeners can always check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for the latest agendas and updates.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Wixom Advances Data Center Limits as Developer Lawsuit Looms
